problem: Embodied-AI research needed a simulator that combines near photo-realistic indoor scenes with rich object interaction, many scenes, and a simple API. Mainstream vision is trained on still images and video, real-robot training is slow, costly, unsafe and confined to lab scenes, and competing simulators (iGibson 2.0, Habitat 1.0/2.0, ThreeDWorld, SAPIEN) have few scenes or objects or weak interaction and state support.
motivation: Humans build visual intelligence by interacting with their environment. The authors argue that a scalable, fast and cheap proxy for real-world experiments, with manipulable objects, state changes and causal effects, is needed to train agents that generalize. They also observe that overfitting to small hand-built scene sets (iTHOR, RoboTHOR) is severe, which drives procedural scene generation (ProcTHOR) inside the same framework.
key_idea: AI2-THOR is a Unity-based, Python-controlled interactive 3D platform: hand-modeled interactive objects and scenes, plus procedurally generated houses, multiple robot embodiments, several image modalities and full environment metadata, together form a general testbed for navigation, interaction and vision-and-language research.
insight: The platform's value comes from unifying many things behind one API: interaction (abstracted actions, arm manipulation, object state changes, causal effects), scene scale (120 iTHOR rooms, 89 RoboTHOR apartments, 10 ArchitecTHOR houses, effectively unlimited ProcTHOR houses) and embodiments (ManipulaTHOR, Stretch RE1, LoCoBot, Abstract, Drone). This is what let one simulator support ImageNav/ObjectNav, ALFRED, TEACh, DialFRED, sim2real and multi-agent work. The paper stresses that environment metadata (poses, visibility, reachable grid, shortest paths) should usually be hidden from the agent and used only to build rewards, experts and datasets, since exposing it would make tasks trivially solvable by heuristics. Its appendix also argues that raw single-process simulator speed is a misleading metric: model forward/backward passes, parallelism and expensive scene resets (handled with synchronized scene-switch tricks) dominate real RL training throughput.
method: Python-Unity agent-simulator loop: actions issued from the Python API are sent through a local server to the Unity engine, which returns an Event containing camera images and environment metadata.

Scene datasets: iTHOR (120 artist-built rooms: kitchens, living rooms, bedrooms, bathrooms); RoboTHOR (89 maze-style dorm apartments, some physically rebuilt in Seattle for sim2real); ProcTHOR-10K (10K procedurally generated houses for training); ArchitecTHOR (10 artist-built houses, 5 val / 5 test).

Agents/embodiments: ManipulaTHOR and Stretch RE1 with arm-based grasping and opening; LoCoBot, Abstract and Drone with abstracted high-level interaction (Open/Pickup succeeds if the object is visible and within a distance).

Action families: navigation (discrete or continuous, e.g. MoveAhead 0.25 m, RotateRight 30°, LookUp 30°, teleport); interactive actions (abstracted, arm-based, object state changes such as slice/cook/break/fill/toggle, causal interactions); environment queries (shortest path to object, object at pixel, convex hull); environment state changes (randomize materials/lighting, resolution, skybox).
Rendering and assets: RGB, depth, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation and surface normals from any camera, extra cameras such as top-down, and 3,578 hand-modeled interactive objects.

Environment metadata per step: agent and object poses and states (visible, open fraction, clean/dirty, moving), scene bounds, 3D bounding boxes, reachable grid positions and action success. Intended for reward shaping, imitation-learning experts and dataset construction rather than as agent input.

Throughput profiling: ObjectNav training with the ProcTHOR actor-critic policy on 2 RTX 2080 GPUs (one for the policy, one for 28 parallel simulator processes), 500-step episodes without an End action, rollout length 128, synchronized scene change every 10 rollouts; compared against Habitat 1.0 with HM3D.

setting.backbone: n/a (simulator platform); throughput benchmark used the ProcTHOR actor-critic ObjectNav policy
setting.training_data: none (platform paper); the profiling agent trained 1M steps of ObjectNav on ProcTHOR-10K
setting.observation: configurable: egocentric RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, normals (plus optional extra cameras); metadata available but usually hidden from the agent
setting.action_space: embodiment-dependent: discrete or continuous MoveAhead (e.g. 0.25 m), Rotate (e.g. 30°), Look (e.g. 30°), teleport, arm control, abstracted interactions (open, pickup, push, throw, drop, place, slice, toggle, etc.)
setting.privileged: none (platform; exposes GT metadata, shortest paths and reachable grid, but these are meant for reward/expert construction, not agent input)

numbers_note: Simulator/platform paper with no navigation benchmark results for any method. The only quantitative result is a throughput comparison: ObjectNav training on ProcTHOR-10K reached 145.5–179.4 training FPS (167.7 average) on a 2-GPU RTX 2080 machine, versus Habitat 1.0 (HM3D) at 119.7–264.3 FPS (230.5 average) under the same setup. Table 1 is a qualitative feature comparison of simulators.
results: No task-performance results are reported. The paper describes the platform: 3,578 interactive objects, 120 iTHOR rooms, 89 RoboTHOR apartments, 10 ArchitecTHOR houses, and effectively unlimited scenes via ProcTHOR. Table 1 claims it is the only simulator in its comparison supporting object states, arm manipulation, multi-agent, sound, VR and an interactive editor. It reports use in over 150 publications and over 500k downloads. In ObjectNav training throughput it averages 167.7 FPS, versus 230.5 FPS for Habitat 1.0 under a matched 2-GPU setup.
limitations: Training throughput is lower than Habitat 1.0 in the paper's own benchmark (167.7 vs 230.5 average FPS), and scene resets are expensive, requiring synchronized scene-switch tricks.

Scenes are synthetic artist-built or procedurally generated rather than scanned real homes, so a visual sim2real gap remains (studied separately in RoboTHOR). The simulator comparison table is self-reported and qualitative.
Abstracted interactions (success if the object is visible and within a distance) simplify low-level control, so results using them may not transfer to physical manipulation.
builds_on: Target-driven visual navigation (Zhu et al. 2017, original THOR)
